title: Test day seven
hook: review the week: Zengzi looked back every day, and Confucius told an overthinker that twice may do
tomorrow: why did Moses carry the broken stones too?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: missing. The gap in the rule, and the rabbis' riddle: the world lacked rest. Today the test week ends, and it's time to look back.

Some people send a text the second they think of it. Others draft it in their notes, rewrite it, rewrite it again, and send it the next morning, or never. Confucius heard about a man like the second kind: Ji Wenzi, a senior minister of Lu from the generation before his, who was known for thinking three times before he acted. The Analects gives his answer, in James Legge's translation: "Twice may do."
screen: `SEND IT NOW, OR DRAFT IT AGAIN?` → `A MINISTER WHO THOUGHT THREE TIMES.` → `TWICE MAY DO.`

segments.voice: So how much looking back is enough? The Analects holds two voices. The first is Zengzi, one of Confucius's students: "I daily examine myself on three points." Was I faithful to the people I worked for? Was I sincere with my friends? Did I practice what I was taught? The same honest questions, every day. On this view, review is how a person is formed: you look back steadily, or you drift. The second voice is the Master's own, about Ji Wenzi. Thinking three times had stopped being wisdom. The later commentator Zhu Xi read it this way: by the second look, what's right is usually clear, and the third look is where worry and self-interest creep in. On that view, reviewing can become a place to hide from acting. Zengzi asks you to look back every day. Confucius warns that looking can turn into stalling. Elsewhere the Analects pictures the noble person as slow to speak and earnest in doing, so in this tradition reflection serves action. A test week's review can hold both voices: the honest questions, asked once, maybe twice, and then a decision.

segments.voice: Take a pen and write the week's review in two passes only. First pass: what worked, and what didn't. Second pass: the one change you'll carry into draft two, then set the pen down, even if a third pass is tempting.
Test day seven: the day you look back over the whole test week, honestly, and then decide. In the Analects, twice may do.
Hold onto this: reviewed, twice and then done. Day 1697, and the test week is over.

howItsDone: In the Confucian tradition, self-examination is a daily habit (Analects 1.4), held together with the Master's warning against endless deliberation (5.19). On a personal rule, a test week usually ends with a short written review and one change for the next draft.
